summary: This week brought a confluence of whistleblower reckonings and archival revelations that underscored both the stakes and the friction within UAP disclosure efforts. Luis Elizondo described a congressional staffer's warning that officials had plans to "eliminate" him, while separately neither confirming nor denying his own past involvement in government secrecy operations, adding another layer of ambiguity to his public role as a disclosure advocate. Meanwhile, lawmakers continued pushing for release of the 1952 "Invasion of Washington" UFO tape, with recent reporting suggesting it may finally surface as part of broader congressional pressure. The Pentagon and military intelligence agencies remained publicly stumped by recurring UAP incursions over bases, while newly released AARO documents examined everything from Starlink satellite flaring to forced perspective effects on UAP observations. Fresh developments also raised questions about whether figures like Elon Musk had been read into classified programs, and experts stressed that without legal protections for whistleblowers, the current disclosure momentum could stall under institutional pressure and retaliation.
